title: Connotation Practice 2
subject: rla
passage:
TEXT A - Local Paper

The paper describes the new plaza as lively; a complaint letter calls it noisy.

TEXT B - Science Summary

The article says a plant invaded the wetland after being introduced from another region.

TEXT C - Coach Feedback

The coach called the team eager rather than impatient.

TEXT D - Housing Article

The writer calls a narrow apartment cozy.

questions.prompt: How do the two words differ?
questions.explanation: Both can refer to activity and sound, but lively approves while noisy criticizes.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: They differ mainly in formality, while expressing essentially the same attitude toward the plaza.
options.whyWrong: The important difference is evaluative: “lively” is favorable, while “noisy” is unfavorable.

options.text: They show that the plaza was busier at one time of day than at another.
options.whyWrong: Both words describe the same plaza activity from different attitudes; the text gives no time-of-day comparison.

options.text: They refer to different sources of activity, with “lively” describing people and “noisy” describing machinery.
options.whyWrong: The passage does not assign the words to different sources; both frame the same active plaza differently.

options.text: They frame similar activity positively and negatively.

questions.prompt: Which word would be most neutral?
questions.explanation: Busy describes activity with less emotional judgment.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: vibrant
options.whyWrong: “vibrant” describes the opposite effect from the one supported by the passage.

options.whyWrong: “deafening” uses a related idea, but the relationship or conclusion does not match the text.

questions.explanation: Invaded is a loaded word that frames the spread negatively.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: harmful or aggressive spread
uncertainty about whether the plant is really present
options.whyWrong: The word expresses an attitude toward the spread; it does not signal uncertainty about the observation.

options.text: carefully managed spread into a new habitat
options.whyWrong: “Invaded” suggests unwanted or aggressive expansion, not controlled introduction.

options.text: a brief seasonal appearance that will probably disappear on its own
options.whyWrong: “Invaded” does not imply the spread is temporary; its negative force suggests the opposite direction.

questions.prompt: How would spread into change the effect?
questions.explanation: Spread into describes movement without the same hostile association.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: It would make the plant sound less harmful but more certain to remain permanently.
options.whyWrong: “Spread into” is more neutral, but it does not establish permanence.

options.text: It would make the sentence more precise about how quickly the plant moved.
options.whyWrong: The replacement changes emotional force, not the stated speed of spread.

options.text: It would sound more neutral.
It would make the plant sound more threatening because “spread” implies loss of control.
options.whyWrong: “Invaded” carries the stronger threatening connotation; “spread into” softens it.

questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: nervous anticipation about whether the team is prepared
options.whyWrong: Nothing in “eager” or the context establishes anxiety.

options.text: negative impatience presented as a problem the coach wants corrected
options.whyWrong: The coach deliberately chooses “eager” instead of “impatient,” giving the behavior a positive frame.

options.text: positive enthusiasm
neutral readiness without any positive or negative judgment
options.whyWrong: “Eager” is positively evaluative rather than neutral.

questions.prompt: Why would impatient be more negative?
questions.explanation: Impatient evaluates the same readiness more critically.
questions.rule: Use the exact wording and surrounding context as evidence.

options.text: It suggests difficulty waiting or controlling frustration.
It suggests the team wants to begin sooner, but without implying any difficulty controlling that desire.
options.whyWrong: “Impatient” specifically adds the negative implication that waiting is difficult or frustrating.

options.text: It makes the coach sound more certain that the team will perform well.
options.whyWrong: The word describes attitude toward waiting, not confidence in performance.

options.text: It removes the coach’s judgment and makes the description more neutral.
options.whyWrong: “Impatient” adds a more negative judgment than “eager.”
